title: MB8-10701
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that they are persons described in Article 1E of the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and her minor son, XXXX XXXX, are Haitian citizens. They are appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that they are persons described in Article 1E of the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. They are neither refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The appellants are appealing against that decision for the following reasons: * The RPD breached procedural fairness by drawing a negative inference from the amendment they made to the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form); * The RPD erred by finding that they enjoy substantially the same rights and obligations as Brazilian citizens; * The RPD erred in the assessment of their forward-looking risk in Brazil.
Having considered all the evidence, I find that the arguments submitted on appeal are unfounded and that the RPD rendered the correct decision.
The appeal is dismissed.

In her first BOC Form, the appellant alleges that they had problems in Haiti in the spring of 2015 because her husband was a member of the Unité [Unity] political party. Fearing for their safety, the appellant, her husband and their young son left for the Dominican Republic on XXXX XXXX, 2015. Given that Haitians were facing a precarious situation in that country, they went to Brazil.

During the first year, the situation in Brazil was rather peaceful. However, after a while, Brazilians allegedly started to threaten Haitians. Some Brazilians reportedly recommended that the appellant and her husband refrain from filing a complaint.

The appellant and her husband decided to leave Brazil in XXXX 2016. They arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2016. The appellant's husband was allegedly deported to Haiti. The appellants stayed in the United States for approximately 10 months before they came to Canada. They claimed refugee protection on August 2, 2017.

On March 2, 2018, they sent the RPD an amendment to their BOC Form, adding allegations concerning the situations in Haiti and Brazil. With respect to Brazil, the appellant added that she had been attacked and that she had a miscarriage because she was pregnant at the time of the incident.

On February 20, 2018,1 the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada requested that the refugee protection claims of the appellant and her son be rejected on the ground that they are persons described in Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, which states: This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.
The appellant was appointed as the designated representative for her minor son. He is basing his refugee protection claim on that of his mother.

In the appeal memorandum, it is submitted that the issues before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) are as follows: * Did the RPD err by drawing a negative inference with respect to the amendment made to the initial BOC Form? * Did the RPD err by finding that the appellants enjoy substantially the same rights and obligations as Brazilian citizens? * Did the RPD err in the assessment of the appellants' fear in Brazil?
I agree that these are the issues that must be reviewed.

Except in cases where the credibility of oral evidence is at issue and the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage, the RAD must determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.2 If I owe deference to the RPD because it enjoys a meaningful advantage, I will indicate it in my analysis. ANALYSIS Breach of procedural fairness

The appellant filed the first BOC Form on August 16, 2017. On March 2, 2018, the appellant made some amendments to the BOC Form by adding that an employee at her work, who was jealous of her, was fired because she was not doing her job well. The latter had plotted with her husband and two other people to beat her up near her workplace. The appellant was four months pregnant and lost the child she was carrying.
The RPD drew a negative inference from the omission of this incident in the initial BOC Form.

The appellants submit that the RPD violated principles of natural justice and procedural fairness because the panel was biased and acted in a manner contrary to legitimate expectation. They argue that rule 9 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules (RPD Rules) allows a refugee protection claimant to change or add information to their BOC Form. According to the appellants, the RPD breached procedural fairness by drawing a negative inference because they failed to mention the attack in the initial BOC Form.3

With respect, I do not share the appellants' point of view. It is not wrong to consider the omission of material facts in the initial BOC Form. The circumstances and the nature of the additions can influence the credibility of the alleged claims.

In this case, the RPD asked the appellant about the omission and considered her explanations, but it found them unsatisfactory. I do not believe that the RPD erred in this case, even if the RPD Rules allow amendments to be made to the BOC Form. It should be noted that the incident omitted was a targeted attack that resulted in a miscarriage, which is not an immaterial fact. I would point out that the appellants have been represented by a lawyer since the beginning of the refugee protection claim process.
The omission of this element from the initial BOC Form was not considered in isolation; the RPD carefully reviewed other aspects of the testimony related to this incident.

In this regard, the RPD noted that the appellant was unable to state when the attack took place. Furthermore, her statements that she was no longer able to work for the company or that she worked as a merchant after the attack contradict the information in the IMM-5669 form, which indicates that she worked as a housekeeper for the same company from XXXX 2015, the date of her arrival in Brazil, until XXXX 2016, the date of departure from Brazil. In addition, there is no indication that she allegedly had another job.

Finally, this is not the only omission. At the hearing, the appellant testified that she had received veiled threats from her neighbour when she complained to her that her son allegedly hurt hers. However, these threats were not included in the initial or amended BOC Form.

When considered together, I find that these omissions from the initial BOC Form cast serious doubt in the decision-maker's mind. Did the Refugee Protection Division err by finding that the appellants enjoy substantially the same rights as Brazilian citizens?

The appellants submit that the RPD decision in this regard is not intelligible and that it is [translation] "completely inconsistent with the evidence." Their memorandum states that: [translation] The appellants are not challenging the fact that they obtained permanent residence in Brazil; the epicentral issue in this case is whether the appellants enjoyed or enjoy all the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country and whether the fears in that country are founded."4 [emphasis added]

The appellants cite Rrotaj v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) 2016 FC 152 and submit that, in their case, renewing permanent residence is contingent on having employment. As a result, Haitians do not have "status substantially similar to that of nationals in that country."5
The RPD did not err by finding that the appellants have permanent resident status in Brazil and, therefore, enjoy substantially the same rights and obligations as Brazilian citizens.

First, contrary to what is being argued, the appellants do not have to enjoy all the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country. The right of return, the right to work freely without restrictions, the right to study, and access to health and social services are rights that must be protected.6

The documentary evidence indicates that foreigners who live in Brazil enjoy substantially the same rights and obligations as nationals.7 On this subject, the information found at Tab 3.4 of the National Documentation Package (NDP) on Brazil (January 31, 2018) indicates that the Constitution of Brazil guarantees foreigners living in Brazil the same rights as Brazilian citizens in terms of access to health care, education, social security and security. The most important restrictions to the rights of foreigners are the prohibition of military service and vote and the veto to some important public office positions.

The RAD's role is to determine whether the RPD erred. It must decide whether, on the day of the hearing, the refugee protection claimant enjoyed substantially the same rights and obligations as Brazilian nationals, in this case, the right of return to Brazil.8

The appellants left Brazil in June 2016. The hearing before the RPD took place on March 14, 2018. On that date, the appellants could have returned to Brazil given that a person does not lose their residency unless they are absent from the country for a period of more than two years. Renewal of their status
The appellants submit that they had residency that is valid for five years and that when the time comes to renew it, they will have to prove that they have a job.
With respect, I disagree with the appellants. The evidence does not lead me to find that their status is valid for only five years. Here is why.
First, their permanent resident card is valid for nine years. It was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and expires on XXXX XXXX, 2025.

The documentary evidence indicates that after the earthquake in Haiti, the Brazilian authorities decided that Haitians required a type of special permit that would allow them to stay in Brazil. Temporary for five years at first, the humanitarian visa became a special permanent status for people whose names (43,871 Haitians) were included on the list attached to the ministerial act of November 2015, which states: [translation] Whereas, pursuant to Normative Resolution No. 97 of January 12, 2012, the (CNIg) invoked humanitarian and compassionate grounds to justify the immigration of Haitians to Brazil following the earthquake in Haiti on January 12, 2010. Furthermore, considering the reception and the social insertion of Haitians in Brazil, the president of the National Committee for Refugees (CONARE) DECIDES, the president of the National Immigration Council (CNIg) AUTHORIZES, and the director of the department of foreign nationals of the justice secretariat GRANTS permanent residence to all individuals on the list attached to this ministerial act.9

According to the information in the Haiti Libre news website:10 "This regularization law grants a one-year deadline for beneficiaries to seek some identification papers abroad," said Miguel Rossetto, stressing that "This residence permit is very important because it prevents immigrants to have to first apply for a temporary visa and because it gives them a perspective of permanent residence so that they can live and enjoy all the rights of a foreigner in Brazil." According to the Minister of Justice Cardozo "permanent residency offers to the Haitians of new job opportunities, social integration and participation in government assistance programs."

Apart from the time required to produce the necessary documents, such as a birth or marriage certificate, two photographs, a criminal record excerpt and application fees, the granting of permanent residence is not subject to any other requirements.

Even if the appellants had temporary status when they arrived in Brazil on XXXX XXXX, 2015,11 they were granted permanent, if not indefinite, residence. Their names are on the list of 43,871 Haitian nationals who were granted permanent residence by the Brazilian authorities in November 2015. Their passports were stamped with "Registrado como permanente" by the federal police on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016.

These elements lead me to find that the appellants have permanent, if not indefinite, status. The fact that the card must be renewed in nine years is not an indication that the status is temporary. Sources indicated to the Research Directorate of the RPD that the validity of the permanent residence is indeterminate but that it must be re-issued periodically, currently at nine-year intervals. ... [R]e-issue of permanent residence is automatic and there is no question of re-application or re-qualification.12
The information found at Tab 3.12 of the NDP and the Ministry of Justice's website indicates that foreigners with permanent status have a foreigner identity card valid for a period of nine years.13

For these reasons, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err by finding that they have permanent, if not indefinite, status and that the rights attached to this status are substantially similar to those of Brazilian nationals. Did the Refugee Protection Division err in the analysis of the forward-looking risk in Brazil?
The appellant submits that: * The RPD erred in reviewing her and her son's forward-looking risk.

As previously mentioned, the RPD noted that due to inconsistencies in the evidence, which had not been adequately explained, it did not believe that the appellant had been attacked. It also states that the omission in her written statements regarding the physical assault against her son led to the finding that this incident had not occurred.
In my opinion, the inconsistencies in the evidence lead me to find that the appellant failed to conclusively establish that these incidents took place.

The RPD did not err by finding that the appellant failed to establish that she and her son face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, in particular for her ethnicity or race, even on cumulative grounds.

The RPD acknowledged that there is racism and discrimination in Brazilian society against Haitians and black people. As the documentary evidence indicates, Brazil is a mixed and diverse country. The report by the Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues suggests that the situation of Afro-Brazilians is complex and that each case must be assessed in light of each individual situation.

The documentary evidence also states that a significant percentage or even most of the Brazilian population identifies as a member of a visible minority group. The Country Report on Human Rights Practices states: The law prohibits racial discrimination, specifically the denial of public or private facilities, employment, or housing, to anyone based on race. The law also prohibits the incitement of racial discrimination or prejudice and the dissemination of racially offensive symbols and epithets, and it stipulates prison terms for such acts. The 2010 census reported that for the first time white persons constituted less than half the population; approximately 52 percent of the population identified themselves as belonging to categories other than white. Despite this high representation within the general population, darker-skinned citizens, particularly Afro-Brazilians, frequently encountered discrimination. Afro-Brazilians were underrepresented in the government, professional positions, and middle and upper classes. They experienced a higher rate of unemployment and earned average wages below those of whites in similar positions. There was also a sizeable education gap. Afro-Brazilians were disproportionately affected by crime; according to one congressional investigative report, black men were 3.7 times more likely to be homicide victims than their white counterparts.14

Paragraph 54 of the UNHCR Handbook states: Differences in the treatment of various groups do indeed exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. Persons who receive less favourable treatment as a result of such differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution. This would be so if measures of discrimination lead to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature for the person concerned, e.g. serious restrictions on his right to earn his livelihood, his right to practise his religion, or his access to normally available educational facilities.15
Professor James C. Hataway and the courts16 have defined persecution as a "sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection."
In this case, I am of the opinion that the appellants failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution if they were to return to Brazil.
Lastly, I cannot ignore that I am surprised by the information in the male appellant's BOC Form that his father, the appellant's husband, lives in Belo Horizonte in Brazil.

In summary, the appellant failed to establish "that there was a sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection" or that there would be a serious possibility that her or her son's fundamental rights would not be recognized if they were to return.
For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination that the appellants are persons described in Article 1E of the Convention.
They are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

The appeal is dismissed.
